title: From Sokółka’s Ghetto to the Deportation Trains
summary: The book’s accounts of persecution, deportation, and murder are essential to understanding both the community’s fate and the purpose of its memorial.

![Sokółka, the town whose Jewish community was destroyed](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Sok%C3%B3%C5%82ka%2C_zesp%C3%B3%C5%82_ko%C5%9Bcio%C5%82a_par._p.w._%C5%9Bw._Antoniego%2C_2_po%C5%82._XIX_01.jpg/1920px-Sok%C3%B3%C5%82ka%2C_zesp%C3%B3%C5%82_ko%C5%9Bcio%C5%82a_par._p.w._%C5%9Bw._Antoniego%2C_2_po%C5%82._XIX_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)
## Occupation and confinement

The destruction of Sokółka’s Jews unfolded through successive measures: occupation, forced labor, confinement, removal to transit camps and deportation. For the [Sokółka Jewish community](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_7ff6fd2ae75c09a88e55a665), the ghetto was not a single episode but a tightening sequence of restrictions that separated people from their homes, livelihoods and one another.

The memorial book’s accounts differ in how they describe the German return. One recalls German troops entering on June 23, 1941, the morning after Germany declared war on the Soviet Union; another places the “second German occupation” in 1941 without specifying the day. The book describes an initial period of requisitions and persecution, followed by orders that Jews wear identifying marks, restrictions on movement and forced labor. The wider chronology likewise places German troops’ return in June 1941, after the Soviet occupation that began in 1939. The community was caught once more in the upheaval of the shifting front: this time under a German regime that turned persecution into a program of confinement and destruction. ([Memorial book, “Sokółka Under the Nazi Yoke”](/communities/sokolka/records/event_candidate_19d9c98dc19d99738114de32); [“German entry and persecution”](/communities/sokolka/records/event_candidate_b1a7d1143d44053e98921912); [Virtual Shtetl’s Sokółka history](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/s/852-sokolka/99-history/138052-history-of-community); [Sokółka, English Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sok%C3%B3%C5%82ka))

The memorial book remembers the [Sokółka ghetto](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_16de72441f26520be9690ce6) as a cramped, walled district in the southern part of town, with its boundaries recalled through local landmarks: the area of Bad-Gesl and the approach at Kondzinski. A witness describes families crowding into rooms, synagogues and study houses turned into living quarters, and the old cemetery left beyond the walls. In its place, residents buried their dead in a courtyard inside the ghetto. The [Southern part of Sokółka](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_d7217752bed9ce5003709fd5) was thus transformed from a familiar part of town into a guarded enclosure. Independent accounts also place the ghetto in autumn 1941 and describe thousands of Jews from Sokółka and nearby communities held there. The exact boundary descriptions vary, but both the book and outside histories convey the same essential fact: confinement compressed an already threatened population into a small, controlled space. ([Memorial book, testimony of Haya Leah Kaplan](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_16de72441f26520be9690ce6); [Virtual Shtetl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/s/852-sokolka/99-history/138052-history-of-community))

## Work, aid and daily survival

Inside the ghetto, work could offer a temporary reprieve, but not safety. The book describes labor selections in which people assembled at the marketplace while employers chose those considered strong and healthy. It also records a [felt factory](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_7b671d3bf5862ce0f429e623), employing about 200 men, and a [shoemaking workshop](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_0b90903a006de9859e2c668f) producing military orders. The workshops were in the ghetto; their workers were useful to the German authorities, but that usefulness did not protect them indefinitely. A selection for work could determine who stayed behind for a time, not who would ultimately live.

The [Judenrat](/communities/sokolka/records/event_candidate_1eac29155ef596df55446935) was formed from prominent townspeople. Accounts name attorney Friedberg, Yosef Broide, Moshe Broide and Gottstein among those associated with it; the records do not present a single, consistent list or leadership description. They describe the council as working under German demands, including the organization of labor and compliance with orders. One episode recalls Friedberg proposing ransom money in the hope of reversing a removal order; accounts differ over the circumstances and response. Such details belong to the book’s testimony, not to a simple portrait of choice: under occupation, Jewish communal bodies faced orders backed by force, while trying to navigate conditions imposed by their persecutors.

The same testimonies preserve efforts to care for one another amid hunger, overcrowding and disease. A doctor and hospital served the ghetto’s sick; a witness describes medicines and food obtained through smuggling and support paid for by people who could afford it. Some patients were transferred to a hospital in [Białystok](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_f19fa262e3d446566a240656), according to the supplied records. The accounts also remember ordinary acts of sharing: neighbors dividing scarce provisions rather than hoarding them. These details do not soften the violence. They show how people tried to preserve communal life under conditions designed to strip it away.

## October, November and the conflicting dates

The date of the main removal is not consistent across the evidence, and it should not be forced into false precision. One supplied event record places a selection and removal in mid-October 1942. Yet a memorial-book witness describes the decisive roundup on November 2: after an announcement that tradespeople might register for work, residents were ordered to the ghetto entrance, where German personnel separated those permitted to remain from those sent away. The book’s introductory text gives January 18, 1943, as the date Jews were gathered in the town square and taken on their “last journey.” Virtual Shtetl’s account says the ghetto lasted until January 24, 1943. These dates may refer to different stages—the first mass removal, the liquidation of the remaining workers and the final dissolution of the ghetto—but the records provided do not resolve every discrepancy. ([Memorial book, “The Last Days of Jewish Sokółka”](/communities/sokolka/records/event_candidate_d9c904241c42748ec3a914f9); [Virtual Shtetl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/s/852-sokolka/99-history/138052-history-of-community); [Memorial book’s introduction](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/sokolka/sok009.html))

The book remembers people driven from their homes under guard and transported first to [Klabasyn](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_8c7c713612ca45f4316fef13), also rendered Kiełbasin or Kelbasin, near Grodno. The transfer was part of a regional system: Virtual Shtetl likewise identifies Kiełbasin as a destination for Sokółka Jews and describes the ghetto’s population as including people from neighboring towns. The book’s account of the [return of remaining Sokolkans from Kelbasin](/communities/sokolka/records/event_candidate_936b66a64d11219937ceb4f3) says that on January 15, 1943, those still in Grodno were taken back to Sokółka. That return did not mean rescue. It preceded further removals and renewed danger.

## Deportation and destruction

The destinations named in the testimony include [Treblinka](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_ea928a786d8d38fcf85de942) and [Auschwitz](/communities/sokolka/records/mention_fd6d37624f20acfc67a74a2c). The records do not establish that every deportee went to the same place or by the same route. In one account, a transport from Kiełbasin went toward Auschwitz; the witness remembers people jumping from a train and being injured near Sokółka. Another record states that on January 23, 1943, 400 men from the factory were deported to Auschwitz and that six survived. This is a specific claim in the memorial-book material, not a total accounting of those deported from the town.

The book’s broader testimony describes mass murder and the destruction of a community that had numbered thousands. A memorial text names German Nazis and Polish collaborators in its accusation. That language expresses the writers’ grief and judgment; it should be read as the book’s voice, not as a complete account of individual responsibility. Independent descriptions confirm the larger pattern of confinement, transfer to Kiełbasin and deportation to killing centers, while differing over dates and final routes. They also place Sokółka within a regional catastrophe in which local ghettos were connected by forced movements and transports. ([Sokółka, English Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sok%C3%B3%C5%82ka); [Virtual Shtetl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/s/852-sokolka/99-history/138052-history-of-community))

The last account is not of a return to ordinary life, but of a town emptied of its Jewish community. The [destruction and murder of Sokółka’s Jews](/communities/sokolka/records/event_candidate_b6798cf652f40e5119900efc) is remembered alongside the specific names and places that make the history legible: Friedberg, the workshops, the ghetto’s streets, Kiełbasin and the deportation destinations. H. L. Kaplan’s testimony, preserved in the book, and the memory of Tamara Schneiderman’s deportation to Treblinka point toward lives that cannot be reduced to a single roundup date or transport. The surviving accounts bear witness to what happened, but they do not encompass every person, route or fate. The records supplied here leave open questions about the final transports, the identities of many victims and the lives of relatives who may have survived elsewhere.
